prompt_free_text:
This paper studies sample efficiency in safe reinforcement learning and proposes ESPO, a primal-style safe policy optimization method that combines a three-mode update rule with adaptive sample-size manipulation driven by reward-cost gradient conflict. The central idea is intuitive: when reward and safety gradients conflict, use more samples to estimate a better compromise direction; when they align, reduce sampling to save interactions and computation. The paper also claims convergence guarantees in a tabular softmax setting and empirical gains on Safety-MuJoCo and Omnisafe benchmarks.

Overall, the paper addresses an important problem. Sample inefficiency is indeed a major bottleneck in safe RL, and adaptive sampling is a natural but underexplored direction in this area. The use of gradient conflict as a signal is also conceptually appealing and connects nicely to recent work in multi-objective optimization and safe RL. The empirical claims, if fully substantiated, would be meaningful: reducing samples while improving both reward and safety would be a strong contribution. However, in its current form, I find the paper promising but not yet fully convincing. The main concerns are about technical clarity, correctness/consistency of the algorithm description, the strength and specificity of the theoretical claims, and the completeness of the empirical validation.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the motivation. The authors correctly identify that fixed sample budgets per iteration are often wasteful in safe RL, especially because the optimization landscape changes across training and because reward-safety tradeoffs are not equally difficult at all times. The three-mode decomposition inherited from PCRPO is reasonable, and using gradient conflict to decide whether to increase or decrease sample size is a plausible heuristic. This is one of the more interesting parts of the paper: unlike variance-only adaptive sampling rules, the proposed criterion is task- and objective-aware. That perspective could be valuable beyond this specific algorithm.

That said, the novelty should be characterized more carefully. The optimization backbone appears to be largely PCRPO-style three-mode optimization plus a sample adaptation heuristic. If that is the main algorithmic novelty, the paper should be explicit that the contribution is not a fundamentally new safe RL optimizer, but rather an adaptive sampling layer on top of an existing primal framework. That is still worthwhile, but the current presentation sometimes overstates the conceptual leap. In particular, the paper repeatedly suggests broad theoretical advances, but the actual theory seems confined to a tabular softmax setting and appears to rely heavily on existing CRPO-style analysis.

A major issue is that the algorithm description contains apparent inconsistencies. In Section 4.1, Equation (3) is described as the update used when gradients conflict, and Equation (4) when they are aligned. But in Section 4.3, the mapping seems reversed: for soft violations with gradient angle less than or equal to 90 degrees, the text says the policy is updated according to Equation (3), while for angle greater than 90 degrees it says Equation (4). This is not a minor typo, because it changes the core logic of the method. If the algorithm description is inconsistent in the main text, it becomes difficult to assess either the theory or the experiments. This must be corrected unambiguously, ideally with pseudocode in the main paper rather than only in the appendix.

Relatedly, the sample manipulation rule is underspecified. Equations (6) and (7) define the sample size as X + X zeta_t^+ or X + X zeta_t^-, but the paper never clearly explains how zeta_t^+ and zeta_t^- are chosen in practice, what ranges they lie in, whether they are deterministic functions of the angle, whether they depend on training stage, or how sensitive performance is to them. Without this, the method is not reproducible and the claimed gains are hard to interpret. If these parameters are hand-tuned per environment, then the sample-efficiency improvements may partly reflect additional tuning effort. The paper needs a precise operational definition of the adaptive sampling schedule.

The theoretical section is another mixed point. It is good that the authors attempt formal analysis, and convergence in a constrained RL setting is nontrivial. However, the theory as presented in the main text is too high-level to support the strongest claims. Theorem 4.1 gives a convergence rate matching CRPO in a tabular softmax setting. This is useful, but it does not by itself establish that adaptive sampling improves sample complexity in the practical deep RL setting used in experiments. In fact, the theorem seems to show that ESPO does not lose convergence guarantees relative to CRPO, rather than proving a sharper rate due to sample manipulation. Proposition 4.3 is especially weak as stated: it says ESPO needs fewer samples than the version without sample manipulation to meet target gaps, but the statement shown in the main text is qualitative and does not provide an explicit bound, dependence on problem parameters, or conditions under which the improvement holds. A comparative proposition without a concrete complexity expression is difficult to evaluate rigorously.

Similarly, Proposition 4.2 on reduced oscillation sounds appealing, but the assumptions seem strong and somewhat opaque. The statement depends on adaptively choosing the parameters x_t^r and x_t^c and on existence of an iteration entering the safe region. It is not clear whether these conditions are guaranteed by the algorithm or are existential. If the proposition requires favorable adaptive choices not specified by the practical method, then its relevance is limited. More generally, the theory appears to analyze the three-mode optimization framework more than the adaptive sampling mechanism itself. The paper should separate clearly what is inherited from PCRPO-style updates and what is genuinely new due to sample manipulation.

There is also a mismatch between theory and practice. The theory is for tabular softmax policies with natural policy gradient style updates and policy evaluation iterations T_pi, while the experiments are on continuous-control benchmarks with neural policies. This is common in RL papers, but then the claims should be calibrated. Statements such as “theoretically guarantees convergence, optimization stability, and improved sample complexity bounds” are too broad unless the paper explicitly says these guarantees hold only in the tabular setting under specific assumptions. As written, the abstract and introduction overgeneralize.

On the empirical side, the reported results are encouraging but not yet sufficiently complete. The paper compares against CRPO, PCRPO, PCPO, CUP, and PPOLag, which is a reasonable set of baselines spanning primal and primal-dual methods. The sample-count reductions in Tables 1 and 2 are substantial. However, the presentation lacks enough detail to judge fairness. For example, are all methods trained until a fixed environment interaction budget, or until convergence, or until a reward threshold? If ESPO uses fewer samples because it stops earlier based on some criterion, then the stopping rule must be identical or equivalently justified across methods. Otherwise, “uses fewer samples” may simply reflect different termination conditions rather than better sample efficiency.

The training-time comparisons are also difficult to interpret. ESPO changes sample counts, but it may also incur extra overhead from computing both reward and cost gradients, gradient angles, and projection operations. The paper notes that sample reduction does not necessarily translate directly to time reduction, which is fair, but then the timing protocol should be carefully specified: same hardware, same number of parallel workers, same implementation framework, same logging overhead, same rollout/evaluation frequency. This is especially important because the paper compares methods across two different benchmark ecosystems, Safety-MuJoCo and Omnisafe, which may have different engineering characteristics.

Another empirical weakness is the lack of visibility into the adaptive mechanism itself. Since the main contribution is sample manipulation, the paper should show how sample sizes evolve over training, how often the algorithm enters each mode, how often gradient conflict is detected, and whether larger conflict indeed correlates with larger benefit from more samples. Without such diagnostics, it is hard to know whether the proposed mechanism is doing meaningful adaptive control or whether the gains come mostly from a favorable average sample budget. A strong ablation would compare: fixed small sample size, fixed large sample size, random sample adaptation with the same average budget, variance-based adaptation, and the proposed conflict-based adaptation. The current text mentions ablations in the appendix, but the main paper should include at least one direct comparison isolating the contribution of the conflict signal.

I also found the safety evaluation somewhat underdeveloped. The paper repeatedly says some baselines “struggle to ensure safety,” but the exact metric is not clearly summarized in the main text. Is safety measured by average episodic cost, discounted cumulative cost, peak violation, fraction of unsafe episodes, or cumulative training-time violations? In safe RL, these distinctions matter a lot. A method that satisfies final-policy constraints but incurs many unsafe interactions during training is very different from one that is safe throughout learning. Since the paper emphasizes deployment relevance, it should report both final constraint satisfaction and safety during training, ideally with confidence intervals and violation statistics.

The experimental scope is decent but still somewhat narrow for the strength of the claims. Only a few tasks are discussed in the main text, and some results are deferred to the appendix. Given that adaptive sampling may be especially sensitive to task difficulty and gradient noise, it would be useful to see broader coverage or at least a clearer rationale for task selection. In addition, because the method relies on gradient angle estimation, robustness to noisy gradient estimates should be tested. For example, what happens when the angle estimate is unstable early in training? Is there hysteresis or smoothing? Could the method oscillate sample sizes due to noisy conflict detection? These are important practical questions.

There are also several writing and presentation issues. The paper has many grammatical errors and awkward phrases, and some sections are repetitive. More importantly, notation is occasionally confusing. The sets B_r, B_soft, and B_c are introduced with labels that do not seem to align perfectly with the mode names. The use of “Safety Violation Response (mode 1), Soft Constraint Violation Response (mode 2), and No Violation Response (mode 3)” together with B_r, B_soft, and B_c is unintuitive, since one might expect B_r to correspond to reward mode and B_c to cost mode. This should be cleaned up. There are also typographical issues such as missing operators or malformed equations in the rendered text. These may seem minor, but in a theory-heavy paper they materially affect readability.

To strengthen the paper, I would suggest the following concrete revisions. First, fix the algorithmic inconsistencies and provide complete pseudocode in the main paper, including exact definitions of zeta_t^+, zeta_t^-, x_t^r, x_t^c, and how gradient angles are estimated from sampled trajectories. Second, sharpen the theory by stating explicit assumptions and making clear which guarantees are new and which are inherited. If Proposition 4.3 can be turned into an explicit sample complexity comparison with concrete dependence on conflict frequency or mode occupancy, that would substantially improve the contribution. Third, expand the empirical analysis of the adaptive mechanism itself: trajectories of sample size, conflict angle histograms, mode occupancy, sensitivity to adaptation parameters, and comparisons to simpler adaptive baselines. Fourth, clarify the safety metrics and report both training-time and final-policy safety. Fifth, ensure fairness in sample/time comparisons by clearly specifying stopping criteria and computational setup.

In summary, I think the paper has a good problem focus and an intuitively appealing idea, and the preliminary empirical results are promising. However, the current version falls short of the rigor expected for a top-tier ML conference because the core algorithm is not described consistently, the adaptive sampling rule is insufficiently specified, the theoretical claims are broader than what is actually established, and the empirical evidence does not yet isolate the contribution convincingly enough. I would encourage the authors to revise substantially, as there is potentially a solid paper here if the method is clarified and the evidence is strengthened.

My overall assessment is borderline to weak reject in its current form: promising idea and potentially useful practical contribution, but not yet sufficiently precise or convincing on theory, algorithm specification, and empirical validation.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes Efficient Safe Policy Optimization (ESPO), a primal-based safe RL method that augments a PCRPO-style three-mode update scheme with adaptive sample-size manipulation. The core idea is to use the angle between reward and safety gradients as a signal: increase samples when gradients conflict and reduce samples when they align or when only one objective is active. The paper claims theoretical guarantees on convergence, reduced oscillation, and improved sample efficiency, and reports empirical gains on Safety-MuJoCo and Omnisafe benchmarks in reward, constraint satisfaction, sample count, and training time.
strengths: Addresses an important practical issue in safe RL: on-policy sample inefficiency under safety constraints.
The high-level intuition is reasonable: gradient conflict may indicate harder optimization regions where more accurate gradient estimates are useful.
Builds on a clear three-mode optimization framework that distinguishes severe violation, soft violation, and safe regions.
Includes both theoretical and empirical components, and evaluates against both primal and primal-dual baselines.
Reported empirical results suggest meaningful reductions in total samples and wall-clock training time on several benchmark tasks.
weaknesses: The paper's central adaptive-sampling mechanism is underspecified. The adjustment parameters zeta_t^+ and zeta_t^- are introduced abstractly, but no concrete rule, schedule, bounds, or implementation details are given in the main text for how they are computed online.

There is a serious inconsistency in Section 4.3: for soft constraint violations with angle <= 90 degrees, the text says to use Equation (3), while Section 4.1 states Equation (3) is for conflicting gradients with angle > 90 degrees; similarly, for angle > 90 degrees Section 4.3 assigns Equation (4), reversing the earlier definition. This creates ambiguity about the actual algorithm.

The theoretical analysis appears disconnected from the claimed contribution of adaptive sample manipulation. The main convergence theorem is for a tabular softmax setting with policy evaluation iterations, but the adaptive sample-size rule itself is not quantitatively characterized in the theorem statement.

Proposition 4.3 is too vague to substantiate the sample-efficiency claim: it states ESPO needs fewer samples than a version without sample manipulation, but no explicit sample complexity bound, dependence on zeta_t^+/zeta_t^-, or comparison rate is provided in the visible statement.

The empirical evidence is not sufficiently rigorous from the provided text: the paper mainly reports total sample counts and qualitative curve claims, but does not clearly specify statistical significance, number of seeds, variance bars, or whether baselines were retuned under equal compute/sample budgets.

Comparisons across primal and primal-dual methods may not be fully fair because ESPO changes the total number of environment interactions while baselines appear to use fixed budgets; stronger evidence would require matched-budget comparisons and/or anytime performance analysis.
The practical overhead of computing both reward and cost gradients and their angle each iteration may offset some efficiency gains, but this tradeoff is not carefully analyzed.

The claimed novelty is somewhat incremental relative to PCRPO plus adaptive batch-size ideas from stochastic optimization; the main new ingredient is the use of gradient conflict as a sampling signal, but the paper does not convincingly isolate why this criterion is superior to simpler uncertainty/variance-based rules.
methodological_flaws: Algorithmic inconsistency: Section 4.3 reverses the mapping between gradient-angle cases and update Equations (3) and (4) relative to Section 4.1. This is not a minor typo because it changes whether projected conflict-handling or direct weighted summation is used.

The sample manipulation rule is scientifically incomplete. Equations (6)-(7) only define X_t = X + X zeta_t^+ or X + X zeta_t^- without specifying admissible ranges, adaptation law, dependence on observed gradients, or safeguards ensuring integer, positive, and stable sample sizes.

The convergence theorem does not clearly prove benefits from adaptive sampling. It establishes a CRPO-like rate in a tabular setting, but the theorem statement does not expose how adaptive sample sizes enter the bound or improve it over fixed-sample variants.

Proposition 4.2 relies on 'adaptively choosing' weights (x_t^r, x_t^c) to guarantee staying in the soft/safe region after entering it. This is a strong existence-style statement unless a constructive rule is given; without such a rule, the optimization-stability claim is weaker than presented.

Proposition 4.3 lacks empirical-validity-level precision as a theorem: it asserts fewer samples are needed to reach target gaps, but no explicit complexity expression or assumptions are visible, making the claim difficult to verify or compare against prior work.

The theory is limited to tabular softmax policies, whereas experiments are in deep continuous-control benchmarks. The paper does not adequately bridge this gap or justify why the theoretical conclusions should support the practical deep-RL implementation.

Empirical validity is weakened by insufficient reporting detail in the provided text: no clear seed counts, confidence intervals, hyperparameter tuning protocol, or matched-budget evaluation are described, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported 25-29% sample savings and 21-38% training-time reductions.
